gloss: To take someone into police custody because they are suspected of a crime.
examples: Police can *arrest* you for driving drunk.
They *arrested* two men outside the bank.
He was *arrested* on Friday and released the next morning.
contrast: You are *arrested* **for** a crime and **on** a charge: *arrested for theft*.

gloss: To hold someone in official custody, often without charging them yet.
examples: Officers may *detain* a suspect for questioning.
Customs *detained* her for two hours.
The protesters were *detained* overnight and let go.

gloss: To lock metal rings around someone's wrists so they cannot use their hands.
examples: Officers *handcuff* a suspect before putting him in the car.
They *handcuffed* him to the railing.
He sat *handcuffed* in the back seat for an hour.

gloss: To question someone closely and for a long time, especially about a crime.
examples: Detectives *interrogate* suspects in a small locked room.
They *interrogated* him for six hours.
She refused to speak while being *interrogated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (patrol the border), intransitive (patrol at night)
gloss: To move regularly around an area to watch for trouble.
examples: Two officers *patrol* this neighborhood at night.
The guards *patrolled* the fence all evening.
A police car was *patrolling* the parking lot.
contrast: Double the *l*: *patrolled*, *patrolling* — the stress is on the last syllable.

gloss: To enter a place suddenly and in force in order to search it or make arrests.
examples: Agents sometimes *raid* houses at dawn.
Police *raided* the club and made twelve arrests.
The warehouse had been *raided* the week before.

gloss: To run your hands quickly over someone's clothing to look for weapons or drugs.
examples: An officer may *frisk* you if he suspects a weapon.
They *frisked* everyone at the door.
He was *frisked* on the sidewalk and then let go.

gloss: To take a record of the patterns on someone's fingertips.
examples: They *fingerprint* everyone who is booked.
The police *fingerprinted* him at the station.
All the applicants are being *fingerprinted* this week.

gloss: To catch and arrest someone who is wanted by the police.
examples: The sheriff hopes to *apprehend* the suspect within days.
Border agents *apprehended* him near the river.
The robbers were *apprehended* at the airport.

gloss: To hold someone back physically, or to stop them by law from doing something.
examples: Two guards had to *restrain* him.
The officer *restrained* the man until backup arrived.
A judge signed an order *restraining* him from contacting her.
contrast: You *restrain* someone **from** doing something; the court paper is a *restraining order*.

gloss: To officially order someone to appear in court or at an official place.
examples: A judge can *summon* any witness in the case.
They *summoned* her to appear on Monday.
He has been *summoned* for jury duty twice this year.
contrast: The verb form *he summons* looks like the noun *a summons* — the court paper itself.

ru: вызывать повесткой в суд, требовать по повестке
gloss: To order someone by law to give evidence or hand over documents.
examples: Prosecutors can *subpoena* your phone records.
The committee *subpoenaed* three witnesses.
He was *subpoenaed* to testify in June.
contrast: The *b* is silent: suh-PEE-nuh. The past keeps the *a*: *subpoenaed*.

gloss: To watch over a person or place in order to keep it safe or stop an escape.
examples: Marshals *guard* the courtroom door.
Two officers *guarded* the evidence room all night.
The building is *guarded* around the clock.
contrast: The *u* is silent: GAHRD.

ru: преследовать в судебном порядке, привлекать к суду
gloss: To bring a criminal case against someone in court.
examples: The state will *prosecute* him for fraud.
They *prosecuted* the company under federal law.
Shoplifters will be *prosecuted*, the sign says.
contrast: Do not confuse *prosecute* (take to court) with *persecute* (treat cruelly).

gloss: To argue in court on behalf of the person who has been accused or sued.
examples: A lawyer will *defend* you even if you cannot pay.
She *defended* him at the trial last spring.
He is *defending* himself without an attorney.
contrast: You *defend* someone **against** a charge; the American noun is *defense*, British *defence*.

gloss: To give someone professional advice, especially legal advice.
examples: Attorneys *counsel* their clients before every hearing.
He *counseled* her to accept the plea deal.
Families are *counseled* free of charge at the courthouse.
contrast: American English keeps one *l*: *counseled*, *counseling* (British *counselled*). *Counsel* (advise) is not *council* (a group of people).

gloss: To state that someone has done something wrong before it has been proven.
examples: The lawsuit *alleges* that the bank hid its fees.
She *alleged* that he had threatened her.
The complaint *alleging* fraud was filed in March.
contrast: As an adjective before a noun, *alleged* usually has three syllables: uh-LEJ-id thief.

transitivity: both — transitive (the judge ruled the evidence inadmissible), intransitive (the court ruled against the city)
gloss: To make an official decision as a judge or a court.
examples: The judge will *rule* on the motion tomorrow.
The court *ruled* in favor of the tenants.
Two appeals judges have *ruled* against the company.
contrast: A court *rules* **on** a question and *rules* **for** or **against** a side.

gloss: To examine someone's case in a court of law.
examples: The state wants to *try* him as an adult.
They *tried* the case in federal court.
He is being *tried* for armed robbery.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *tries*, *tried*. You are *tried* **for** a crime.

transitivity: both — transitive (adjourn the hearing), intransitive (the court adjourned)
gloss: To stop a meeting or a court session, usually until a later time.
examples: The judge may *adjourn* the hearing until Friday.
Court *adjourned* at four o'clock.
The trial was *adjourned* for the holidays.
contrast: The *d* is silent: uh-JURN.

gloss: To talk something over carefully before reaching a decision, as a jury does.
examples: The jury will *deliberate* behind closed doors.
They *deliberated* for three days.
While the jurors were *deliberating*, the families waited outside.
contrast: The verb ends in -rayt; the adjective *deliberate* ('on purpose') ends in -ruht: di-LIB-uh-ruht.

gloss: To formally argue that a decision, a bill or a document is wrong.
examples: You can *contest* a parking ticket in court.
She *contested* her father's will.
The result is being *contested* by both sides.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-TEST; the noun *contest* ('a competition') is KAHN-test.

gloss: To formally question whether something is legal or correct.
examples: Lawyers can *challenge* a juror without giving a reason.
The city *challenged* the ruling right away.
The law is being *challenged* in federal court.

gloss: For a higher court, to let a lower court's decision stand.
examples: The appeals court may *affirm* the sentence.
The judges *affirmed* the lower court's decision.
His conviction was *affirmed* last month.

transitivity: both — transitive (litigate a claim), intransitive (they litigated for years)
gloss: To take a dispute through the courts instead of settling it.
examples: Most companies would rather settle than *litigate*.
They *litigated* the patent for a decade.
The case is still being *litigated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (mediate a dispute), intransitive (mediate between two sides)
gloss: To help two sides reach an agreement without a trial.
examples: A retired judge will *mediate* the dispute.
She *mediated* between the two families for months.
Their divorce was *mediated* out of court.
contrast: You *mediate* **between** two sides.

gloss: To make information known that was secret or that the law requires you to share.
examples: The law requires banks to *disclose* every fee.
He never *disclosed* the payments to his employer.
The documents were *disclosed* to the defense.

gloss: To officially show that someone accused of a crime is not guilty.
examples: New evidence could *exonerate* him.
DNA tests *exonerated* two of the men.
He was fully *exonerated* after eleven years in prison.

gloss: To make someone look guilty of a crime.
examples: You never have to *incriminate* yourself.
The recording *incriminated* both partners.
They found *incriminating* emails on his laptop.

gloss: To show that someone was involved in a crime or a wrongdoing.
examples: His testimony could *implicate* the mayor.
The report *implicated* three officers.
She was *implicated* in the cover-up but never charged.
contrast: Someone is *implicated* **in** a crime.

ru: объявлять импичмент, выдвигать обвинение против должностного лица
gloss: To formally charge a public official with serious misconduct in office.
examples: The House can *impeach* a president or a federal judge.
Lawmakers *impeached* the governor in 2009.
He was *impeached* but not removed from office.
contrast: Verbs ending in *-ch* add *-es*: *impeaches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (she divorced him), intransitive (they divorced last year)
gloss: To legally end a marriage.
examples: They may *divorce* before the end of the year.
She *divorced* him after twelve years.
My parents have been *divorced* since I was six.

gloss: To state officially and in writing that something is true or correct.
examples: A notary can *certify* the copy for you.
The state *certified* the election results on Monday.
Send a *certified* copy of the birth certificate.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *certifies*, *certified*.

gloss: To have a notary officially witness and stamp a signature.
examples: You have to *notarize* the signature before you mail it.
The bank *notarized* the document for free.
Send us the *notarized* form by Friday.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*: *notarize*, *notarized*.

gloss: To kill a person on purpose and against the law.
examples: Prosecutors say he planned to *murder* his business partner.
Someone *murdered* the night clerk in 1998.
Two witnesses were *murdered* before the trial began.

transitivity: both — transitive (kill a man), intransitive (drunk driving kills)
gloss: To cause a person or an animal to die.
examples: Drunk driving *kills* thousands of people every year.
The single shot *killed* him instantly.
Four people were *killed* in the crash.

gloss: To murder an important public figure, usually for political reasons.
examples: Extremists tried to *assassinate* the judge.
A gunman *assassinated* the senator in 1968.
The candidate was *assassinated* two weeks before the vote.
contrast: Two pairs of double letters: a-*ss*-a-*ss*-inate.

gloss: To attack someone physically, which is a crime in itself.
examples: It is a felony to *assault* a police officer.
He *assaulted* a guard during the arrest.
She was *assaulted* on her way home from work.

transitivity: both — transitive (attack a driver), intransitive (the dog attacked without warning)
gloss: To try to hurt someone by using violence.
examples: He insists the dog did not *attack* anyone.
Someone *attacked* him with a bottle.
The victim was *attacked* from behind.
contrast: Two *t*'s, then *-ck*: *attacked*, *attacking*.

gloss: To kill someone by squeezing their throat so they cannot breathe.
examples: The defense claims he did not *strangle* her.
The attacker *strangled* the victim with a cord.
She had been *strangled*, the coroner said.

gloss: To cause someone severe pain on purpose, often to force information out of them.
examples: The treaty forbids any state to *torture* prisoners.
Guards *tortured* the detainees for months.
He says he was *tortured* while in custody.

gloss: To take a person away by force and hold them, usually for money.
examples: They planned to *kidnap* the banker's son.
Two men *kidnapped* her outside the store.
The boy was *kidnapped* in 2011 and found a year later.
contrast: Double the *p*: *kidnapped*, *kidnapping*.

gloss: To take someone away illegally by force.
examples: Someone tried to *abduct* a child from the playground.
They *abducted* him at gunpoint.
She was *abducted* and held for three days.

gloss: To take control of a plane, a ship or a truck by force.
examples: Two men tried to *hijack* the plane.
Thieves *hijacked* a truck full of electronics.
The bus was *hijacked* just after midnight.

gloss: To attack someone in a public place and rob them.
examples: Someone could *mug* you in that alley.
They *mugged* him for his phone.
She has been *mugged* twice this year.
contrast: Double the *g*: *mugged*, *mugging*.

gloss: To keep bothering or threatening someone over a period of time.
examples: Debt collectors may not *harass* you at work.
He *harassed* two coworkers for months.
She was *harassed* online after the trial.
contrast: One *r* but two *s*'s: *harass*, *harasses*, *harassed*.

gloss: To frighten or hurt a weaker person again and again.
examples: Older kids *bully* him on the bus.
They *bullied* her until she changed schools.
He was suspended for *bullying* a classmate.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *bullies*, *bullied*. The vowel is the short *uu* of *put*.

gloss: To treat a person cruelly, or to use power or a substance wrongly.
examples: It is a felony to *abuse* a child.
He *abused* his position to win contracts.
She had been *abused* for years before she called the police.
contrast: The verb ends in a *z* sound, uh-BYOOZ; the noun *abuse* ends in *s*, uh-BYOOS.

gloss: To fail to take care of someone or something you are responsible for.
examples: Landlords who *neglect* repairs can be fined.
The court found that she had *neglected* the children.
The building had been *neglected* for years.

gloss: To put someone or something in a dangerous situation.
examples: Drunk drivers *endanger* everyone on the road.
The gas leak *endangered* the whole block.
He was charged with *endangering* a child.

gloss: To leave a person, an animal or a thing that you are supposed to care for.
examples: In this state it is illegal to *abandon* a pet.
She *abandoned* the car on the highway.
The children had been *abandoned* by both parents.

transitivity: both — transitive (shoplift a jacket), intransitive (caught shoplifting)
gloss: To steal goods from a store while pretending to be a customer.
examples: Teenagers sometimes *shoplift* on a dare.
She *shoplifted* a lipstick and got caught at the door.
He was arrested for *shoplifting* twice in one month.

gloss: To break into a building in order to steal from it.
examples: Thieves *burglarize* empty houses in the summer.
Someone *burglarized* our garage last night.
Three stores were *burglarized* on the same block.
contrast: American English says *burglarize*; British English says *burgle*.

transitivity: both — transitive (loot a store), intransitive (crowds began to loot)
gloss: To steal from shops or homes during a riot, a war or a disaster.
examples: Crowds began to *loot* the stores downtown.
They *looted* a pharmacy during the blackout.
The shop was *looted* and then set on fire.

gloss: To move goods or people secretly and illegally across a border or into a place.
examples: They use tunnels to *smuggle* cigarettes.
He *smuggled* a phone into the prison.
The drugs were *smuggled* across the border in a truck.

transitivity: both — transitive (traffic weapons), intransitive (traffic in stolen art)
gloss: To trade illegally in drugs, weapons or people.
examples: Agents say the pair *traffic* in fake passports.
He *trafficked* heroin along the coast for years.
She was arrested for *trafficking* weapons.
contrast: A *k* appears before the ending: *trafficked*, *trafficking* — like *panic → panicked*.

gloss: To make an exact copy of money or goods in order to cheat people.
examples: It is a federal crime to *counterfeit* money.
They *counterfeited* designer bags for years.
The bills had been expertly *counterfeited*.
contrast: The ending sounds like *-fit*, not *-feet*: KOWN-tur-fit.

transitivity: both — transitive (plagiarize an article), intransitive (students who plagiarize)
gloss: To copy someone else's words or ideas and present them as your own.
examples: Students who *plagiarize* can be expelled.
He *plagiarized* half of the report.
Two paragraphs had been *plagiarized* word for word.

transitivity: both — transitive (hack a server), intransitive (hack into a system)
gloss: To break into a computer system without permission.
examples: Criminals can *hack* a small bank in minutes.
Someone *hacked* my email last night.
The hospital's records were *hacked* in the spring.
contrast: With no direct object, you *hack* **into** a system.

gloss: To cheat a person or an organization out of money.
examples: They used fake invoices to *defraud* the state.
He *defrauded* investors of nine million dollars.
Hundreds of customers were *defrauded* before the site closed.
contrast: You *defraud* someone **of** their money.

gloss: To trick someone into giving you money or personal information.
examples: Callers try to *scam* older people every day.
They *scammed* her out of her savings.
He has been *scammed* twice online.
contrast: Double the *m*: *scammed*, *scamming*.

gloss: To steal money that your employer or your organization has put in your care.
examples: A treasurer can *embezzle* money for years unnoticed.
She *embezzled* four hundred thousand dollars from the church.
The missing funds had been *embezzled* by a manager.

gloss: To give someone money or gifts so that they will act dishonestly for you.
examples: You cannot *bribe* a federal judge.
They *bribed* an inspector to sign the permit.
He admitted *bribing* two city officials.
contrast: The silent *e* drops before *-ing*: *bribing*.

gloss: To demand money or favors by threatening to reveal a secret.
examples: He threatened to *blackmail* his own boss.
She *blackmailed* him with the photos.
They had been *blackmailing* him for months.
contrast: You *blackmail* someone **into** doing something.

gloss: To get money from someone by using threats or force.
examples: The gang tried to *extort* money from shop owners.
He *extorted* thousands from his neighbors.
The payments had been *extorted* under threat.
contrast: You *extort* money **from** someone.

gloss: To touch or change something you have no right to touch, in order to damage or falsify it.
examples: No one may *tamper* with a witness.
Someone *tampered* with the lock.
He was charged with *tampering* with evidence.
contrast: *Tamper* always takes **with**.

gloss: To arrange a contest, a vote or a machine dishonestly so the result is fixed.
examples: They tried to *rig* the bidding.
He *rigged* the machines to pay out less.
The contest had been *rigged* from the start.
contrast: Double the *g*: *rigged*, *rigging*.

gloss: To deceive someone into doing or believing something.
examples: Scammers *trick* people into sharing their passwords.
They *tricked* her into signing the papers.
He felt *tricked* by the whole agreement.
contrast: You *trick* someone **into** doing something.

gloss: To make someone believe something that is not true.
examples: The ads were designed to *deceive* buyers.
He *deceived* his own family for years.
Investors say they were *deceived* about the risk.
contrast: It is *-ei-* after *c*: dec**ei**ve, not *decieve*.

gloss: To harm someone who trusts you, often by handing them over to their enemies.
examples: He would never *betray* a friend.
She *betrayed* the group to the police.
They felt *betrayed* by their own lawyer.
contrast: A vowel before the *y* keeps it: *betrays*, *betrayed*.

gloss: To pretend to be another person in order to deceive people.
examples: It is a crime to *impersonate* a police officer.
He *impersonated* a doctor for two years.
She was charged with *impersonating* a federal agent.

gloss: To control people or figures dishonestly for your own advantage.
examples: Traders can *manipulate* the price of a small stock.
He *manipulated* the records to hide the loss.
The evidence had been *manipulated*.

gloss: To force someone to do something by using threats or pressure.
examples: Police may not *coerce* a confession.
They *coerced* him into pleading guilty.
She says she was *coerced* by her employer.
contrast: You *coerce* someone **into** doing something.

gloss: To damage someone's reputation by saying false things about them out loud.
examples: You cannot *slander* someone and call it an opinion.
He *slandered* his former partner on the radio.
She sued, saying she had been *slandered*.
contrast: *Slander* is spoken; *libel* is written or printed.

gloss: To damage someone's reputation by publishing false statements about them.
examples: A newspaper can *libel* a private citizen just as easily.
The magazine *libeled* him in 2016.
He claims he was *libeled* by the post.
contrast: American English keeps one *l*: *libeled*, *libeling* (British *libelled*).

gloss: To say publicly that someone or something is wrong or criminal.
examples: Leaders were quick to *denounce* the attack.
She *denounced* the verdict as unjust.
He was *denounced* by his own neighbors.

gloss: To tell a deliberate lie in court after swearing to tell the truth.
examples: No witness should *perjure* himself to protect a friend.
She *perjured* herself twice on the stand.
He admitted *perjuring* himself in an earlier case.
contrast: *Perjure* is used only with *myself, yourself, himself, herself*.

gloss: To go onto someone's land or into their property without permission.
examples: Hunters sometimes *trespass* on private land.
He *trespassed* on the same farm twice.
They were arrested for *trespassing* on the tracks.
contrast: You *trespass* **on** someone's property; the sign reads NO TRESPASSING.

gloss: To take part in violent public disorder by a crowd.
examples: Fans sometimes *riot* after a big loss.
Prisoners *rioted* for two nights.
Hundreds were arrested for *rioting*.
contrast: One *t*: *rioted*, *rioting* — the stress is on the first syllable, so nothing doubles.

transitivity: both — transitive (plot an attack), intransitive (plot against the mayor)
gloss: To plan something harmful or illegal in secret.
examples: The men began to *plot* a robbery.
They *plotted* against the mayor for months.
He admitted *plotting* to burn the building.
contrast: Double the *t*: *plotted*, *plotting*.

gloss: To make a secret agreement with others to do something illegal.
examples: Prosecutors say the brothers began to *conspire* in 2019.
They *conspired* to defraud the government.
He was charged with *conspiring* to commit fraud.
contrast: You *conspire* **with** someone **to** do something.

gloss: To deliberately get in the way of an official process.
examples: Lying to agents can *obstruct* an investigation.
He *obstructed* the search by hiding the files.
She was convicted of *obstructing* justice.

gloss: To urge people on to violence or disorder.
examples: Speech that *incites* violence is not protected.
He *incited* the crowd to storm the gate.
They were accused of *inciting* a riot.
contrast: *Incite* (stir up) sounds exactly like *insight* (understanding).

gloss: To break a law, a rule or an agreement.
examples: Parking here would *violate* the city code.
The company *violated* three safety rules.
He went back to prison for *violating* his parole.

transitivity: both — transitive (disobey an order), intransitive (he chose to disobey)
gloss: To refuse to do what a law, an order or a person in authority requires.
examples: Soldiers who *disobey* an order can be court-martialed.
He *disobeyed* the judge's instructions.
She was fined for *disobeying* a police officer.
contrast: A vowel before the *y* keeps it: *disobeys*, *disobeyed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (obey the law), intransitive (he refused to obey)
gloss: To do what a law, a rule or a person in authority tells you to do.
examples: You have to *obey* the court's order even if you appeal it.
He *obeyed* every instruction the officer gave.
She was arrested for not *obeying* a lawful command.
contrast: A vowel before the *y* keeps it: *obeys*, *obeyed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (resist arrest), intransitive (do not resist)
gloss: To fight back against someone trying to control or arrest you.
examples: Do not *resist* if an officer stops you.
He *resisted* and was pushed to the ground.
She was charged with *resisting* arrest.

gloss: To play games of chance for money, which is regulated or banned in many places.
examples: In some states you still may not *gamble* online.
He *gambled* every weekend at the casino.
Three men were caught *gambling* in the back room.

gloss: To treat a person worse than others because of race, sex, age or religion.
examples: An employer may not *discriminate* against older workers.
The bank *discriminated* against buyers in those neighborhoods.
She says she was *discriminated* against because of her accent.
contrast: *Discriminate* takes **against**.

gloss: To punish someone, usually with a fine or a loss of rights.
examples: The IRS can *penalize* you for filing late.
The court *penalized* the firm with a heavy fine.
Drivers are *penalized* for every point on their record.
contrast: The first syllable is PEE-, though the noun *penalty* starts PEN-. American spelling uses *-ize*.

ru: сажать в тюрьму, заключать под стражу
gloss: To put someone in a local lockup, usually for a short sentence or before trial.
examples: A judge can *jail* you for contempt of court.
They *jailed* him for six months.
He was *jailed* while he waited for trial.

gloss: To lock someone up in a prison.
examples: A state may not *imprison* anyone without a trial.
They *imprisoned* him for twenty years.
He had been wrongly *imprisoned* since 1994.
contrast: One *s*, pronounced like *z*: im-PRIZ-uhn.

gloss: To shut someone up in a prison or jail; a formal word common in American reporting.
examples: It costs a state a fortune to *incarcerate* one person.
They *incarcerated* him in a federal facility.
Nearly two million Americans are *incarcerated* today.

gloss: To kill someone as a legal punishment ordered by a court.
examples: Only a few states still *execute* prisoners.
The state *executed* him in 1998.
No one has been *executed* here in a decade.

gloss: To officially forgive a crime and cancel the punishment.
examples: Only a governor can *pardon* a state prisoner.
The president *pardoned* two hundred people.
He was *pardoned* after serving eight years.

gloss: To release a prisoner early on condition of good behavior.
examples: The board may *parole* him next spring.
They *paroled* her after four years.
He was *paroled* in March and violated the terms in June.

gloss: To force a foreign national to leave the country.
examples: The government can *deport* someone who overstays a visa.
They *deported* him to Honduras last year.
Thousands were *deported* before the rule changed.

gloss: To hand a suspect over to another country for trial.
examples: Spain has agreed to *extradite* him.
They *extradited* her to the United States.
He was *extradited* after a two-year fight.

gloss: To force someone officially to leave a school, an organization or a country.
examples: A school can *expel* a student for bringing a weapon.
They *expelled* him in his final year.
Two diplomats were *expelled* from the country.
contrast: Double the *l*: *expelled*, *expelling* — the stress is on the last syllable.

gloss: To legally force a tenant to leave a property.
examples: A landlord cannot *evict* you without a court order.
They *evicted* the family in January.
She is being *evicted* for unpaid rent.

gloss: To punish a member of an organization for breaking its rules.
examples: The department rarely *disciplines* its own officers.
They *disciplined* two guards after the video came out.
He has been *disciplined* three times this year.
contrast: Stress the first syllable, DIS-uh-plin; the last syllable rhymes with *pin*, not *pine*.

gloss: To help an offender change so that they can live a normal life again.
examples: Prisons are supposed to *rehabilitate* people, not just hold them.
The program *rehabilitated* hundreds of young offenders.
He was *rehabilitated* and now speaks in schools.

transitivity: both — transitive (reform the law), intransitive (he has reformed)
gloss: To change a system for the better, or to change your own behavior for the better.
examples: Both parties promise to *reform* the sentencing rules.
The state *reformed* its bail system in 2019.
He is a *reformed* car thief who now teaches teenagers.

gloss: To forbid something officially.
examples: Some cities want to *ban* the sale of these guns.
The court *banned* him from driving for a year.
Fireworks are *banned* inside the city limits.
contrast: Double the *n*: *banned*, *banning*. You are *banned* **from** a place or an activity.

gloss: To forbid something by law or by a formal rule.
examples: Federal law *prohibits* discrimination in hiring.
The lease *prohibited* pets of any kind.
Smoking is *prohibited* in all public buildings.
contrast: You are *prohibited* **from** doing something. The last syllable is unstressed, so nothing doubles: *prohibited*.

gloss: To set limits on what someone may do or have.
examples: The new law will *restrict* who can buy ammunition.
The judge *restricted* his travel to two counties.
Access to the file is *restricted* to the attorneys.
contrast: You *restrict* something **to** a limit.

gloss: To stop something for a time, or to bar someone from a job or a right temporarily.
examples: The board may *suspend* his license.
They *suspended* the officer without pay.
He got a *suspended* sentence and served no time.

gloss: To cancel a permission, a license or a right that was granted before.
examples: The state can *revoke* a driver's license for good.
They *revoked* his bail after the second arrest.
Her visa was *revoked* at the airport.

gloss: To make something lawful that used to be a crime.
examples: Voters may *legalize* sports betting next year.
Colorado *legalized* marijuana in 2012.
Once it was *legalized*, the arrests stopped.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*: *legalize* (British *legalise*).

gloss: To make something illegal.
examples: Congress could *outlaw* the practice tomorrow.
The city *outlawed* smoking in its parks.
Those weapons were *outlawed* in 1994.

gloss: To make sure a law or a rule is obeyed.
examples: Nobody bothers to *enforce* that rule.
The city *enforced* the curfew for three nights.
The speed limit is *enforced* by camera.

gloss: To control an activity by official rules.
examples: Federal agencies *regulate* the sale of firearms.
Congress *regulated* the industry after the crash.
Banks are heavily *regulated* in this country.

gloss: To change the wording of a law, a contract or an official document.
examples: Lawmakers may *amend* the bill this week.
They *amended* the contract twice before signing.
The complaint was *amended* to add two defendants.

gloss: To officially cancel a law so that it no longer applies.
examples: The new majority wants to *repeal* the law.
Congress *repealed* the tax in 2017.
Prohibition was *repealed* in 1933.

gloss: To make a bill into a law.
examples: Several states plan to *enact* similar rules.
The legislature *enacted* the ban in June.
The law was *enacted* over the governor's veto.

gloss: To give formal approval to a treaty or an amendment so that it takes effect.
examples: The Senate must *ratify* the treaty first.
Thirty-eight states *ratified* the amendment.
The agreement has not been *ratified* yet.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *ratifies*, *ratified*.

gloss: For a president or a governor, to refuse to approve a bill.
examples: The governor may *veto* the bill.
He *vetoed* it on the last possible day.
The measure was *vetoed* and never became law.
contrast: The third-person form takes *-es*: *vetoes*.

gloss: To impose an official penalty on a person, a firm or a country.
examples: A judge can *sanction* a lawyer who lies to the court.
The court *sanctioned* the firm ten thousand dollars.
Two banks were *sanctioned* last year.
contrast: *Sanction* has two opposite senses: to punish, and to approve officially. The context decides.

gloss: To rule that someone may not take part or hold a position.
examples: A conflict of interest can *disqualify* a judge.
The court *disqualified* two jurors.
He was *disqualified* from holding office for life.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *disqualifies*, *disqualified*.

gloss: To give someone an official notice of a traffic or parking fine.
examples: They *ticket* cars on this street every morning.
A trooper *ticketed* him for speeding.
She was *ticketed* twice in one week.
contrast: The ending is unstressed, so there is no doubling: *ticketed*, not *ticketted*.

gloss: To take a vehicle or goods into official custody.
examples: The city can *impound* your car for unpaid tickets.
They *impounded* the truck at the border.
His van was *impounded* as evidence.
